title: When the Confession Breaks
premise: Vesper Underhill, a true-crime podcaster with a private habit of solving 'accidents,' is hired by a nervous woman named Ilse Corvane to prove that her husband, a retired police archivist, will not be murdered — a crime she insists has not yet happened. Digging in, Vesper discovers the husband holds the only unredacted copy of a forty-year-old confession that three prior deaths were staged to protect, and that his client may be either the next victim or the killer's accomplice. As Vesper reconstructs the original murder from corrupted records, he realizes the killer is someone inside the investigation itself — and that his own podcast episodes have been feeding the killer the case file. In the end, Vesper stages a fake confession broadcast to lure the killer into destroying the last copy of the document, exposing him live on air, but survives at the cost of his anonymity, his archive, and his certainty about which side of the truth his client stood on.
about_author: Cyrus Vane is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing testimony before turning to fiction. He writes mysteries obsessed with what official records leave out, and lives quietly under a name no one can quite verify.

chapters.title: The Client Who Paid for Nothing
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. A woman named Ilse Corvane hires him to prove her husband won't be murdered — an impossible brief she pays triple for, in cash, up front. Vesper takes it half as a joke, half because the money smells like fear. The beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: An Archive of Accidents
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He researches Aldous Corvane, retired police archivist, and finds a pattern: three people connected to a 1984 case file died in 'accidents' over two decades. The chapter establishes Vesper's method — reading death certificates like confessions. Beat: the thrill of a pattern emerging.

chapters.title: What Aldous Keeps in the Basement
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. The old archivist catalogs his basement, lingering on a sealed box labeled only with a case number. He knows someone has been asking about him; he counts the locks twice. Beat: dread building in an ordinary man who has been waiting thirty years to be found.

chapters.title: The First Interview
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He interviews Aldous, who is charming, evasive, and lets slip one detail — a name redacted from every public record. Vesper recognizes it from his own solved 'accidents.' Beat: the cold realization that his cases are all tributaries of one river.

chapters.title: Episode Forty-Seven
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, intercut with anonymous listener comments. He airs a cautious episode about the 1984 case; within hours, a comment appears quoting an internal evidence log Vesper never had. Someone with access is listening — or steering him. Beat: the hunter realizing he is bait.

chapters.title: Ilse's Version
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. She rehearses her story alone, and small cracks show: she knows too much about the 1984 victim's habits. Her fear seems real, but so does her precision. Beat: the reader begins doubting the client without evidence.

chapters.title: The Retired Detective
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He tracks down Dana Merrick, lead investigator on the 1984 case, now dying in a care home. She gives him a fragment: the confession was never signed; the suspect walked; the file was 'corrected' from inside. Beat: grief and fury at institutional rot.

chapters.title: Accident Number Four
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. A witness Vesper contacted is found dead — a fall on wet stairs, textbook. Too fast, too clean. Vesper understands his inquiries are being read in real time. Beat: guilt curdling into resolve; the case is now his.

chapters.title: The Redaction Pattern
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, deep-work chapter. Comparing the three old deaths, he maps who benefited from each redaction and narrows the leak to someone still employed in records or its orbit. Beat: intellectual exhilaration shadowed by the knowledge that the killer can do the same math.

chapters.title: What Ilse Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He confronts Ilse with inconsistencies; she admits she was married once before — to the 1984 suspect's son. Her request wasn't paranoia; it was a test to see if Vesper could finish what others died starting. Beat: betrayal reframed as recruitment.

chapters.title: The Son
chapters.summary: The son's POV (unnamed). He tends his father, now senile, reading him newspaper clippings that aren't news. The father sometimes confesses in fragments; the son records everything. Beat: chilling tenderness — love weaponized into custodianship of a crime.

chapters.title: Merrick's Last Tape
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Dana Merrick dies before their second meeting, but a nurse delivers a cassette she left: names, dates, and the phrase 'the confession breaks where the family begins.' Beat: a torch passed by a dying hand; stakes become personal.

chapters.title: Following the Money Backwards
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Tracing who paid for the original defense and the subsequent cover-ups, he finds a quiet foundation still funding 'archival preservation' — and a signature he's seen on Ilse's retainer paperwork. Beat: vertigo; the client and the conspiracy share handwriting.

chapters.title: House Call
chapters.summary: Alternating Vesper and Aldous POVs. Vesper returns to warn Aldous; the house feels watched; Aldous finally opens the basement box — empty except for a receipt proving he sold the true confession years ago. Beat: the floor drops out of the case.

chapters.title: The False Confession
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. She confesses her design to herself: she hired Vesper not to prevent a murder but to make the killer believe the confession still existed, forcing him to move against Aldous and expose himself. Beat: moral ambiguity sharpening — she used Vesper as bait knowingly.

chapters.title: Trap Logic
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Furious but clear-eyed, Vesper agrees to the counter-trap: announce on air that he possesses the original confession, and let the killer come for it. He plans the broadcast like a crime scene. Beat: cold determination; the podcaster becomes the instrument.

chapters.title: Episode Fifty-Two: Live
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, real-time tension. He reads a fabricated confession on air, seeded with errors only the true killer would correct. Within minutes, a caller phones in — gently, precisely fixing the details. Beat: triumph and terror in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Man from Records
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Tracing the call, he unmasks the killer: the current custodian of the county archives, who inherited the cover-up as a career and has been 'preserving' it with bodies for decades. Beat: banality of evil revealed in fluorescent-lit mundanity.

chapters.title: Basement Reckoning
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating Vesper and killer POVs. The killer comes for Aldous and the supposed confession; Vesper and Ilse intervene. A struggle amid forty years of paper; the killer nearly burns the archive — and himself — rather than be exposed. Beat: violence, fire, and the physical cost of truth.

chapters.title: After the Recording Stops
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Police arrive to a burned wing, a cuffed killer, and a podcaster holding a recorder full of admissible admissions. But the real 1984 confession is gone forever — destroyed in the fire. Beat: hollow victory; justice served without closure.

chapters.title: What Ilse Signed
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Reviewing her retainer, he finds the signature matching the foundation's — Ilse built the trap to bury her family's guilt along with the killer, using him as the shovel. She vanishes, leaving payment and a single line: 'You proved nothing happened. Thank you.' Beat: bitter clarity about being used well.

chapters.title: The Next Cold Case
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, epilogue. His identity is public now; his archive burned; his audience doubled. He receives a new envelope, postmarked nowhere, containing one page of a confession he's never heard of — and a date next week. Beat: survival's price paid forward; the cycle resumes.
